paragraphs: Air traffic controllers combine flight plans, radar or visual surveillance, and weather and radio reports into a real-time airspace picture, and then maintain safe separation between aircraft with standard control instructions; the workplace is a tower, an approach control facility or an area control centre, and the core measures are safe separation, accuracy of instructions and completeness of handover, not flying an aircraft or running an airport. People worth exploring usually accept sustained monitoring under high-precision rules, communicate in concise phraseology, and are prepared for the handover responsibility and the shift rhythm.

People who are more likely to adapt: those who can hold attention for long periods and stay accurate through repeated instructions, are willing to communicate in standard phraseology and accept read-back verification, can handle situations to procedure under pressure rather than improvising, and can accept night, weekend and shift duty. If sustained concentration is hard, strict procedure and supervision are unwelcome, or the person will not stand down from duty when fatigued or unwell, the risk is usually greater.

In one sentence: a safety-critical post that authorises, sequences and hands over aircraft in a tower, an approach control facility or an area control centre under established procedures, in order to maintain safe separation, issue accurate instructions and record the operating process.

The tasks of air traffic controllers fall into three groups: surveillance and sequencing (continuously monitor the airspace of responsibility with radar, computer equipment or visual reference, predict track crossings and conflicts, and sequence aircraft movement); issuing and handover (issue altitude, heading, speed, runway-entry and take-off and landing clearances, listen to and verify the pilot's read-back, and hand control over to the adjacent tower, approach or area position); and anomalies and coordination (on lost communication, severe weather, runway incursion or an aircraft in distress, issue alerts, adjust the sequence, notify airport emergency services and record the action).

O*NET 53-2021.00 air traffic controllers: control air traffic in and around an airport, and control the flow of air traffic between sectors at various altitudes and between control centres; under established procedures and policy they authorise, regulate and control commercial flights in order to expedite and ensure flight safety. The workplace is a tower, an approach control facility or an area control centre; common job titles include tower controller, approach radar controller, area controller and air traffic control specialist.

The boundary turns on four things: who sets the airspace rules and separation standards, who exercises control within the airspace of responsibility, who flies the aircraft, and who is responsible for the facility and the equipment. Controllers exercise control and provide information to procedure and within the authorisation; flight operations are the pilot's responsibility; airspace rules, separation standards and licence administration are set and overseen by the civil aviation authority; and the installation, scheduled inspection and repair of communication, navigation and surveillance equipment are handled by specialist technical units.

The objects are the aircraft and the flight flow within the airspace of responsibility; the basis is the airspace rules, the separation standards, the control procedures and the licence endorsements.

Air Traffic Controllers (corresponding on the U.S. side to O*NET/BLS 53-2021.00) control air traffic in and around an airport and between sectors at various altitudes and between control centres; under established procedures and policy they authorise, regulate and control aircraft movement in order to expedite and ensure flight safety; the workplace is a tower, an approach control facility or an area control centre. On the mainland China side, civil aviation controllers operate under a licence system: licences are issued and administered centrally by the Civil Aviation Administration of China and are endorsed by category such as aerodrome control, approach control, area control, approach surveillance control, area surveillance control, flight service, operations monitoring and apron control. Four kinds of risk are most worth judging in advance: first, separation and instruction risk (a missed read-back verification, a clearance beyond the authorisation); second, communication and coordination risk (communication degradation, an unclear handover); third, personnel status risk (fatigue and a decline in physiological condition); fourth, data and record risk (over-trusting an automation prompt, an inaccurate or untraceable record). values: AT30 fully fictional paper cards: at 10:00, V1 has six cards, A requests slot 0 confirmed, B slot 1 confirmed, C slot 4 to be verified, D slot 5 confirmed, E slot 7 confirmation blank and F slot 9 confirmed. Slots are arbitrary paper units with no flight, altitude, heading, speed or military data.

Paper rules: only a confirmed card may be sequenced; sequence in increasing request-slot order, where a placed slot = max(request slot, previous placed slot +3), and the first card uses its request slot. 3 is an arbitrary paper constraint set by the author and is emphatically not an aviation safety separation. At 10:10, V2 changes D from confirmed to to-be-verified (a new field is inconsistent, cause unknown); the other cards are unchanged and an existing confirmation may be carried over.

Within 45 minutes produce the six-card V1/V2 state matrix, the two sequences and the adjacent slot differences, the V2 confirmation ratio and the 10:15 handover. At 10:15, A gives only a 'file received' acknowledgement without version or item confirmation; this does not make C/D/E pass, nor does it mean the whole is closed.

It issues no aircraft clearance or control instruction and invents no communication-loss or runway-incursion handling action. The exercise observes information and version verification only and cannot serve as an attention scale, a medical examination, a licence or proof of selection ability.

Reference recalculation: V1 confirms A/B/D/F, 4 in total, C to be verified 1, E blank and missing 1; the sequence is A0→B3→D6→F9 with adjacent differences 3/3/3. V2 confirms A/B/F, 3 in total, C/D to be verified 2, E missing 1; the sequence is A0→B3→F9 with differences 3/6. Each version totals 6; the V2 confirmation rate is 3÷6=50%, which is not an operational success rate or completion of a selection process.

Reference handover: the 10:15 summary cites AT30 V2, lists the six-card input and states, and records that D changes from confirmed to to-be-verified because a new field at 10:10 is inconsistent with the cause undetermined; C is still to be verified and E is blank. The A/B/F paper sequence meets the given 3-unit constraint; A has only received the file, and the to-be-verified and missing items are still unresolved.

Eight-point scoring, 1 point each: ① the complete six cards and the V1 states 4/1/1; ② the D change and the V2 states 3/2/1, plus the carry-over condition for the others; ③ the V1 sequence 0/3/6/9 and the differences 3/3/3; ④ the V2 sequence 0/3/9 and the differences 3/6; ⑤ 3/6=50% as the confirmation rate only; ⑥ C/D to be verified and E missing, with an unknown cause and no fabricated entry; ⑦ the 10:00/10:10/10:15 versions and A's file acknowledgement not closing the loop; ⑧ the paper 3 unit is not an aviation standard and no clearance/instruction/qualification conclusion is issued. Sample A writes only ③, the sequences and differences, omitting the rest, 1/8; sample B copies the complete input matrix and the ①-⑧ deliverables above, 8/8; a mark is not a qualification proof.

entries.answer: This occupation issues instructions within the airspace of responsibility and maintains safe separation; flight operations are the pilot's responsibility; airspace rules, separation standards and licence administration are set and overseen by the civil aviation authority; the installation, scheduled inspection and repair of communication, navigation and surveillance equipment are handled by specialist technical units; and airport facilities and operating-resource coordination belong to adjacent occupations such as airport operations officers.
